title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
description: Lewis Carroll's 1865 dream-tale: a girl falls down a rabbit-hole into a world where size, names and rules keep changing, and keeps asking who she is until she wakes by refusing to be afraid of it.

cover.alt: Alice shields herself as the pack of cards flies at her
cover.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Alice grows and shrinks a dozen times, and every time the question is the same: if my body keeps changing, what part of me is still me?

images.alt: Alice swimming in the pool of tears among birds and animals
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Wonderland is full of rules and has no law. Every creature is certain, and every certainty is invented on the spot.

images.alt: Gardeners painting the white roses red as the Queen arrives
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The dream ends the moment Alice stops taking it seriously. Power that runs on fear falls apart into paper.

images.alt: Alice shields herself as the pack of cards flies at her
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The first real terror of the book is not the fall but the morning after it. Alice runs through the children she knows, trying to work out which of them she has been changed into.
chunks.source_quote: Who in the world am I? Ah, that’s the great puzzle!

images.alt: Alice, curious and a little lost
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The Caterpillar demands the one thing Alice cannot give: a stable account of herself. His curtness is the adult world's, which asks children to explain a self that is still changing size.
chunks.source_quote: “I can’t explain myself, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m not myself, you see.”

images.alt: The Caterpillar on his mushroom, Alice peering up at him
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The Cheshire Cat's logic is airtight and useless: being here proves you are mad. It is the only creature that tells Alice the rules of the place honestly.
chunks.source_quote: “Oh, you can’t help that,” said the Cat: “we’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad.”

images.alt: The Cheshire Cat in its tree, Alice asking which way to go
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The Hatter asks a riddle that has no answer and the party never ends because time has stopped at six o'clock. Conversation becomes a game whose only aim is to keep the other player off balance.
chunks.source_quote: “Why is a raven like a writing-desk?”

images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The trial of the Knave is the book's sharpest satire: evidence that proves nothing, a jury writing down the dates and adding them up, and a Queen who wants the punishment first.
chunks.source_quote: “No, no!” said the Queen. “Sentence first—verdict afterwards.”

images.alt: The trial of the Knave of Hearts
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: By the seaside Alice has stopped panicking about who she is and simply reports it: change is no longer a catastrophe but a fact of the day.
chunks.source_quote: “but it’s no use going back to yesterday, because I was a different person then.”

images.alt: Alice by the sea with the Gryphon and the Mock Turtle
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Gregor Samsa and Alice both wake into bodies that do not fit. Kafka follows the family that stops recognising the son; Carroll follows the child who stops recognising herself, and lets her win by growing back to full size and talking back.

images.alt: The baby turns into a pig in Alice's arms
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: The Hatter's unanswerable riddle and Poe's Raven, which answers every question with the same word, are two sides of one joke about meaning: a question with no answer, and an answer that fits every question.

images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.

chunks.text: Carroll was Charles Dodgson, a mathematics lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford. The book's nonsense is precise: syllogisms with false premises, words taken literally, arithmetic that drifts ("four times five is twelve"). It has been a favourite of logicians, philosophers of language and, later, computer scientists for exactly that reason.

Read as a story about childhood, Wonderland is the adult world seen from below: full of people who give orders, set exams, recite lessons and get angry when you don't know the rules nobody told you. Alice's courtesy is constantly met with rudeness, and most of the book is her learning that politeness is not the same as obedience.

What changes across the book is not Wonderland but Alice. At the start she cries a pool of tears and nearly drowns in it. By the end she is the one who calls the court nonsense, grows to full size in the middle of the trial and dismisses the whole machinery of power as a pack of cards. The dream does not teach a moral, which is the Duchess's joke ("Everything's got a moral, if only you can find it"); it teaches a stance. Identity is not something you settle once. It is something you keep asserting in a world that keeps changing your size.

images.alt: The Duchess's kitchen, full of pepper and flying saucepans
images.credit: Illustration made with gpt-image-2 for ConteXtube.
